paras: The lynching near Osceola, Arkansas, was the killing in 1888 of an unnamed Black man accused of sexually assaulting a white married woman, as reported by the Osceola Times. It is known only from a one-sentence item in a Missouri weekly of November 24, 1888, which gives no date, place, names or account of the killers.

According to the Fair Play of Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, the Osceola, Ark. Times reported "the lynching of a brutal negro who committed a carnal assault on a white married lady." The item states the assault as fact, but no arrest, charge or trial of the man is mentioned. It does not say who carried out the lynching, how many took part, how the man was killed, or where in Arkansas it happened.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The only surviving account is secondhand: the Fair Play printed it on its second page under "General Items," between a note about a St. Louis woman visiting friends and an advertisement for a farm paper. The brief calls the victim "a brutal negro" and the woman "a white married lady," adopting the accusation as fact and offering no comment on the killing itself. No wire version, Arkansas report or follow-up was found, and the Black press of the period is not represented in the coverage.
